extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and readers of poetry/essays (early-18th-century style guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating and critiquing characters (especially in epic poetry) and for tasteful literary composition, drawn from periodical essays and satirical examples. Includes advice on use of source letters, tone in moral criticism, allegory, probability, variety, and reader-relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of correspondents' letters as material
rubrics_metrics.description: I receive a double Advantage from the Letters of my Correspondents, first as they shew me which of my Papers are most acceptable to them; and in the next place as they furnish me with Materials for new Speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters may be used to discover popular topics and to supply raw materials. The writer may transform hints into original plans, change language or thought into their own way of speaking and thinking, and (if it can be done without prejudice to the sense) omit the many compliments and applauses usually bestowed. Also observe subscriber parts at the end of letters as a means to lengthen a paper. Anti-pattern: publishing letters verbatim with flattering compliments that bloat tone or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform source material rather than reproducing praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes indeed I do not make use of the Letter it self, but form the Hints of it into Plans of my own Invention; sometimes I take the Liberty to change the Language or Thought into my own Way of Speaking and Thinking, and always (if it can be done without Prejudice to the Sense) omit the many Compliments and Applauses which are usually bestowed upon me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using reader-submitted material, adapt and synthesize rather than copy. Preserve sense but recast expression; cut extraneous flattery. Scoring note: originality and clarity of adaptation valued over literal reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion about audience-appropriate language
rubrics_metrics.description: If it had been proper for them to hear, they may be sure the Author would not have wrapp'd it up in Greek... I then let drop several Expressions, as if there was something in it that was not fit to be spoken before a Company of Ladies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use learned or foreign-language citations with care; don't cloak indecent or offensive thoughts in erudition to avoid accountability. If content isn't fit for a given audience, avoid presenting it or use discretion rather than veiled obscenity. Anti-pattern: deliberate obscurantism to hide impropriety or to entrap readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deliberately advancing vice even with wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Sallies of Imagination are to be overlooked, when they are committed out of Warmth in the Recommendation of what is Praise worthy; but a deliberate advancing of Vice, with all the Wit in the World, is as ill an Action as any that comes before the Magistrate, and ought to be received as such by the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and imaginative sallies may be forgiven when they praise virtue, but intentionally promoting vice (even cleverly) is ethically culpable. Writers should weigh public effect; rhetorical cleverness does not excuse moral harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine plot (fable) first, then characters (Aristotelian method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Having examined the Action of Paradise Lost, let us in the next place consider the Actors. This is Aristotle's Method of considering, first the Fable, and secondly the Manners; or, as we generally call them in English, the Fable and the Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical method: analyze the plot/structure before analyzing characters. In composition, ensure the action supports and reveals character. Scoring note: coherence between fable and characters is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and novelty of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer has excelled all the Heroic Poets that ever wrote, in the Multitude and Variety of his Characters... there is scarce a Speech or Action in the Iliad, which the Reader may not ascribe to the Person that speaks or acts, without seeing his Name at the Head of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a large range of distinct characters with novel traits suitable to the work's scope. Variety aids reader interest; novelty distinguishes an epic. Example: Homer vs. Virgil — Homer praised for variety and novelty; Virgil criticized for less variety among minor figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make speech and action uniquely identify characters
rubrics_metrics.description: There is scarce a Speech or Action in the Iliad, which the Reader may not ascribe to the Person that speaks or acts, without seeing his Name at the Head of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give each character distinctive manners of speaking and acting so readers can attribute lines without labels. Anti-pattern: flat dialogue or interchangeable actions that blur identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure characters suit the genre and the poem's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in these several Characters of Homer, a certain Dignity as well as Novelty, which adapts them in a more peculiar manner to the Nature of an Heroic Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the dignity, novelty, and behavior of characters to the expectations and scale of the genre (e.g., heroic/epic). A mismatch between character type and genre weakens believability and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid homogeneous minor characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil falls infinitely short of Homer in the Characters of his Poem, both as to their Variety and Novelty... Gyas, Mnesteus, Sergestus and Cloanthus, are all of them Men of the same Stamp and Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate minor characters to avoid monotony. If many characters share the same 'stamp', the poem loses richness. Example anti-pattern: a cast of identical 'men of the same stamp'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility/probability in characterization; caution with allegorical or chimerical beings
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot think that Persons of such a Chymerical Existence are proper Actors in an Epic Poem; because there is not that measure of Probability annexed to them, which is requisite in Writings of this kind...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic characters should observe a degree of probability appropriate to the work. Allegorical or fantastical personifications (e.g., Sin, Death) risk undermining plausibility unless handled carefully. Use allegory sparingly and ensure it coheres with the poem's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory may be effective if imaginatively and properly employed
rubrics_metrics.description: If such empty unsubstantial Beings may be ever made use of on this Occasion, never were any more nicely imagined, and employed in more proper Actions, than those of which I am now speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While allegorical beings can endanger plausibility, they can succeed when imaginatively conceived and put to fitting actions. Scoring note: success depends on quality of invention and appropriateness of function in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose heroes related to the intended readers to elicit sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: I mean the Authors having chosen for their Heroes, Persons who were so nearly related to the People for whom they wrote... By this means their Countrymen...were particularly attentive to all the Parts of their Story, and sympathized with their Heroes in all their Adventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting protagonists who share identity/ties with the target audience (national, cultural) strengthens reader engagement and emotional investment. Anti-pattern: heroes alien to audience risk indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix virtue with infirmity in tragic characters to arouse pity and terror
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Man of perfect and consummate Virtue falls into a Misfortune, it raises our Pity, but not our Terror... If we see a Man of Virtue mixt with Infirmities, fall into any Misfortune, it does not only raise our Pity but our Terror; because we are afraid that the like Misfortunes may happen to our selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragic effect, craft characters who are essentially good but possess weaknesses or errors. Purely perfect characters do not provoke terror; a resemblance to ourselves (flawed virtue) generates both pity and terror. Also: 'a Person of an absolute and consummate Virtue should never be introduced in Tragedy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure divine/supernatural characters act consistently with their nature
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another Circumstance... how has he represented the whole Godhead exerting itself towards Man in its full Benevolence under the Three-fold Distinction of a Creator, a Redeemer and a Comforter!... nothing ascribed to Uriel, Gabriel, Michael, or Raphael, which is not in a particular manner suitable to their respective Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including gods, angels, or other supernatural beings, tailor their speech and behavior to their established roles and dignity. Inconsistency between nature and action undermines credibility and aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate tone when reproving vice; consider mitigating circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling Names does no Good; to speak worse of any thing than it deserves, does only take off from the Credit of the Accuser, and has implicitly the Force of an Apology in the Behalf of the Person accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing moral failings in prose or satire, temper invective with fairness. Assess context (poverty, parental pressure, passion) and vary appellations according to circumstances. Anti-pattern: indiscriminate name-calling which weakens the critic's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the thing, not the person; conceal names when exposing vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The enclosed is sent you, which is verbatim the Copy of a Letter written by a Bawd of Figure in this Town to a noble Lord. I have concealed the Names of both, my Intention being not to expose the Persons but the Thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exposing misconduct, focus on practices and systemic issues rather than sensationally naming individuals. Redact identifying details to avoid libel and keep purpose ethical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, absurd detail in satire to reveal character types
rubrics_metrics.description: An imaginary Operator opened the first with a great deal of Nicety... we found that the Brain of a Beau is not real Brain, but only something like it... The Pineal Gland... smelt very strong of Essence and Orange-flower Water... the Musculi Amatorii, or, as we may translate it into English, the Ogling Muscles, were very much worn and decayed with use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire benefits from vivid, specific, and slightly absurd details (invented anatomy, named 'muscles') that concretely expose follies. Such particulars make caricature memorable and sharpen comic effect. Anti-pattern: vague generalities that fail to pinpoint targets.
